Surah al-Ahzab (The Confederates)
Seventy-three verses, and it is Madani by consensus.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿O Prophet, fear Allah⦆

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾. In explaining this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the difference between the vocative and the one addressed when saying "Ya rajul" (O man) and "Ya ayyuha ar-rajul" (O you, the man). Many things have been said about this, and we say: the utterance "Ya rajul" indicates the act of calling, and his utterance "Ya ayyuha ar-rajul" also indicates that, and it signals the gravity of the matter for which the one addressed is called, or the heedlessness of the one addressed. As for the second, it is mentioned. As for the first: because his saying "Ya ayyu" makes the one addressed unidentified at first, so every listener becomes attentive to the one being called; then when he singles out one person, in that there is a signal to all of them, since they are attentive to him. But if he says "Ya Zayd" or "Ya rajul," only the one mentioned turns to the one being called. Having understood this, we say: "Ayyuha" cannot be taken to indicate the heedlessness of the Prophet, because his saying "the Prophet" (al-Nabi) contradicts heedlessness, since the Prophet, upon him be peace, is aware, and so he is not heedless; therefore it must be taken to indicate the gravity of the matter.

The second issue: a command to do something is only given when the one commanded is not already occupied with the thing commanded, since it is not appropriate to say to one who is sitting, "Sit down," or to one who is silent, "Be silent." The Prophet, upon him be peace, was God-fearing, so what is the meaning here? We say there are two aspects:

The first is transmitted: that he was commanded to persist, for it is correct for one to say to someone sitting, "Sit here until I come to you," and for one to say to someone silent, "You have done right, so be silent and you will be safe," meaning: continue in what you are upon.

The second, which is a subtle rational point: a king is feared by his servants in three ways. Some fear his punishment, some fear the cessation of his reward, and a third group fears his veiling (concealment from him). The Prophet was not commanded to be God-fearing in the first sense nor in the second sense. As for the third, the sincere one does not feel secure from it as long as he is in this world, and how could he, since worldly affairs are preoccupying, and the human being in this world is at times with God, and at other times turned toward what he cannot do without, even if God is with him. An indication of this is his saying: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed﴾ [Fussilat: 6], meaning: the veil is lifted from me

at the time of revelation, then I return to you as though I were one of you. So the command to fear God requires the continuance of presence.

The second aspect: the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, every moment his knowledge and rank were increasing, until his state in the past, in comparison with what he is in now, was a forsaking of the better, so for him there was a renewed God-fearing at every hour. Thus his saying ﴿fear Allah﴾, on this view, is a command to something he did not already have. To this the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, alluded in his saying: "Whoever has two equal days is a loser." Also, he asked his Lord, by God's command to him, for an increase in knowledge, when He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. Also, to this the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, alluded in his saying: "Indeed, there comes over my heart, so I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times a day," meaning: a station is renewed for him in which he says that what he brought of thanks and worship was not anything.

Having understood this, the Prophet ﷺ, by the ruling of ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾, had a slight fear from the tongues of the disbelievers and hypocrites and from their hands, as evidenced by God's saying: ﴿And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. So Allah commanded him a God-fearing beyond what he already had, to the point that it makes him forget creation and he wants nothing but the Truth; and Allah increased his rank by it. Thus this was good news to him in ﴿O Prophet﴾: you, as long as you remain, are in the rank in which you are not content to be given a God-fearing like the God-fearing of ordinary people or the God-fearing of the awliya' (saints); rather, from you nothing is accepted except a God-fearing that makes you forget yourself.

Do you not see that a person who fears the loss of his wealth, if a ruthless man comes upon him intending to kill him, becomes distracted from the wealth and flees and leaves it? Likewise the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, was commanded with this kind of God-fearing, and with this God-fearing no fear of anyone other than God remains. This is expressed in the manner of one who says to someone fearing Zayd or 'Amr: "Fear 'Amr, for Zayd cannot prevail over you while 'Amr is with you." This is not a command to fear 'Amr, for he (already) fears him; rather it is a prohibition against fearing Zayd, implicit in a command to increase fear of 'Amr, until it makes him forget Zayd.

Then His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ confirms what we have said, i.e., fear Allah with a God-fearing that prevents you from obeying them.

The third issue: why were the disbelievers and hypocrites singled out for mention, although the Prophet ﷺ should not obey anyone other than Allah? We say: for two reasons.

The first: mentioning others is unnecessary, because others do not seek from the Prophet, upon him be peace, that he follow them, nor do they expect that the Prophet, upon him be peace, would become obedient to them; rather they intend that he follow them, and they do not regard him as anything but one who is obeyed.

The second: when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾, He forbade him from obeying all; for everyone who asked the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, to obey him is either a disbeliever or a hypocrite, because whoever commands the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, with a command of obligation, believing that if he did not do it he would punish him with right, is a disbeliever.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾, an indication that God-fearing should be from the core of your heart; you should not conceal in yourself the fear of other than Allah, as one does who sees in himself courage while fearing within himself and forcing himself to bear it. For God-fearing is from Allah, and He is Knowing. His saying ﴿Wise﴾ is an indication to repel the illusion of one who imagines: if Allah says something, and all the disbelievers and hypocrites, though they are relatives of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, say something else and see benefit in it and mention a rational reason, then following them would be nothing but benefit. So Allah, exalted is He, said: He is Wise. Benefit is only in the word of the Wise. So when Allah commands you with something, follow it, even if the people of the world forbid you from it.

"And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do." "And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs." "Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest, nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons. That is your saying from your mouths, but Allah says the truth, and He guides to the [right] way."

He confirms what we mentioned, that He is the All-Wise, so following Him is obligatory. Then He said, "Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do." When He said that He knows what is in the hearts of the servants, He explained that He is the All-Knowing, the Acquainted with your deeds. So purify your hearts and correct your deeds.

* * *

Then He said, "And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs." That is, fear Allah, and if you suspect anyone [of harm], then rely upon Allah, for He is sufficient as a protector. With Him, one who benefits does so, and nothing harms when He is with you; and if He harms, nothing benefits in His presence.

* * *

Then He said, "Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest." Some of the exegetes said: the verse was revealed concerning Abu Ma'mar, who used to say, "I have two hearts, and with one of them I understand more than Muhammad understands." So Allah refuted him with His saying, "Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest." Al-Zamakhshari said regarding His saying, "nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers," that it means: He has not made for a man two hearts, just as He has not made for a man a trustee or a son of two fathers. Both of these views are weak. Rather, the truth is to say: when Allah commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to be mindful of Him with His saying, "O Prophet, fear Allah," that was a command to him to a taqwa beyond which there is no taqwa. Whoever is mindful of Allah and fears something with intense fear, nothing else enters his heart. Do you not see that one who is greatly fearful forgets his concerns during the state of fear? So it is as if Allah, exalted is He, said: "O Prophet, fear Allah as He should be feared." And among its due right is that there should not be in your heart any taqwa of other than Allah. For a person does not have two hearts, so that he may be mindful of Allah with one and of another with the other. If he is mindful of another, that can only happen by turning the heart away from the direction of Allah toward another, and that does not befit the one who is mindful who claims that he fears Allah as He should be feared.

Then He mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should not fear anyone at all, nor fear as you feared in the account of Zaynab, the wife of Zayd, when Allah said, "and you feared people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him" [al-Ahzab: 37]. That is: such taqwa should not enter your heart. Then, when He had mentioned the Prophet (ﷺ) in that state, He mentioned what repels evil from him, saying: "nor has He made your adopted sons your sons." That is: Allah has not made the adopted son of a man his son. Then He placed before it what is strong evidence for the removal of the ugliness, which is His saying: "nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers." That is: when you say to your wives, "You are to me like the back of my mother," she does not become a mother to you, by the consensus of all. In Islam, this is because it is zihar, which does not make intercourse unlawful. In the pre-Islamic period (jahiliyya), it was a divorce, to the extent that it was permissible for the husband to marry her again. So if the saying of a speaker to his wife, "You are my mother," or "like the back of my mother," does not necessitate that the wife becomes a mother, then likewise the saying of a speaker to an adopted son, "You are my father," does not necessitate that he becomes a son, so his wife does not become the wife of a son. Thus no one could say anything about that, and your fear of people had no basis. How [could it be otherwise]? For if it were a fearful matter, it would not be permissible for you to fear other than Allah. Or do you not have two hearts, while your heart is occupied with the taqwa of Allah? So it would not be fitting for you to fear anyone.

* * *

Then He said, "That is your saying from your mouths." In this there is a subtle point, which is that meaningful speech is of two kinds.

The first: speech that is about something that exists, so it is said.

The second: speech that is said, so it comes to be as it was said. The first is the speech of the truthful (al-sadiqin), who say what is the case. The second is the speech of the sincere ones (al-siddiqin), who, when they say something, Allah makes it as they said. Both proceed from the heart. Speech that is only by the mouth is like the braying of a donkey or the barking of a dog, because meaningful speech is that which is relied upon, and that which does not come from the heart and deliberation is not relied upon. Allah, exalted is He, when He honored the children of Adam and preferred them over the rest of the animals, it is fitting that one should guard against adopting their characteristics.

So the saying of one who says, "This is the son of so-and-so," while he is not his son, is not speech, for speech is in the heart, and this is only in the mouth. The subtle point is that Allah, exalted is He, here said, "That is your saying from your mouths," and He said regarding His saying: "And the Christians say, 'The Messiah is the son of Allah.' That is their saying from their mouths" [al-Tawbah: 30]. That is, attributing a person to other than his father is a saying that has no reality, does not come out of a heart, and does not enter a heart either. So it is a saying by the mouth, like the sounds of beasts.

* * *

Then He said, "But Allah says the truth." This is an indication of a subtle meaning, which is that the intelligent person should make his saying either from reason or from the sharia. So when he says, "So-and-so is the son of so-and-so," it should be either from reality, or from the sharia, by being his son in the legal sense, even if he does not know the reality. Like one who marries a woman, and she gives birth to a child after six months, and the woman had previously been the wife of another person, and it is possible that the child is from him. We attribute the child to the second husband on the basis of the established marital bed, and we say: he is his son. But in the case of the adopted son, neither the reality exists nor has the sharia come with it, because [Allah] says only the truth, and this is contrary to the truth, because his father is well known and apparent.

There is another aspect to it: they said, "This is the wife of the son," so it is forbidden. Allah said: "She is lawful for you." Their saying has no weight, for it is from their mouths like the sounds of beasts, while the saying of Allah is true, so it must be followed. His saying, "and He guides to the way," confirms His saying, "But Allah says the truth." That is: it must be followed because it is true and because it is guiding.

His saying, exalted is He, "That is your saying from your mouths, but Allah says the truth," contains a subtle point: speech that is only by the mouth resembles the sound of beasts, which arises without a heart. Then, speech of the heart may be true and may be false, for one who says something on the basis of belief may be correct, so it is true, or may not be correct, so it is false. So the saying that is in the heart, which is the one considered from your sayings, may be true and may be false, because it follows existence. But the saying of Allah is true, because existence follows it; for He speaks of what has been, or He says and it comes to be. Therefore the saying of Allah is better than your sayings that come from your hearts, so how could it be compared with your sayings that are from your mouths? Therefore it is not permissible for you to take up your false, idle saying and leave the true saying of Allah. Whoever says that the Prophet's (ﷺ) marriage to Zaynab was not good has abandoned the true saying of Allah and taken up a saying that came out of the mouth [only].

* * *

Then He said, "and He guides to the way." This is an indication that following what Allah has sent down is better than adopting the saying of others.

Their saying has no weight, for it is from their mouths like the sounds of beasts, while the saying of Allah is true, so it must be followed. His saying, "and He guides to the way," confirms His saying, "But Allah says the truth." That is: it must be followed because it is true and because it is guiding.

His saying, exalted is He, "That is your saying from your mouths, but Allah says the truth," contains a subtle point: speech that is only by the mouth resembles the sound of beasts, which arises without a heart. Then, speech of the heart may be true and may be false, for one who says something on the basis of belief may be correct, so it is true, or may not be correct, so it is false. So the saying that is in the heart, which is the one considered from your sayings, may be true and may be false, because it follows existence. But the saying of Allah is true, because existence follows it; for He speaks of what has been, or He says and it comes to be. Therefore the saying of Allah is better than your sayings that come from your hearts, so how could it be compared with your sayings that are from your mouths? Therefore it is not permissible for you to take up your false, idle saying and leave the true saying of Allah. Whoever says that the Prophet's (ﷺ) marriage to Zaynab was not good has abandoned the true saying of Allah and taken up a saying that came out of the mouth [only].

* * *

Then He said, "and He guides to the way." This is an indication that following what Allah has sent down is better than adopting the saying of others.

[Page 168]

Then He explained the guidance, saying: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah. But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients. And there is no blame upon you for that in which you have made a mistake, but [there is blame for] what your hearts intended. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

His saying, ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾: "Call them" means "attribute them to," i.e., be guided [in this]. His saying, ﴿that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾: "more just" means more equitable, for it is placing a thing in its proper place. This [phrase] may be understood in two ways:

The first: that the [word] "their" (the possessive) has been omitted for generality, meaning "more just than every [other] statement," like the saying of the speaker, "Allah is greatest" (Allahu akbar).

The second: that what preceded is intended, as if he said: "That is more just than your saying, 'He is the son of so-and-so.'" Then he completed the guidance and said: (﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients﴾, meaning: say to them, "our brothers" and "the brother of so-and-so." If they were freed [slaves], then say: "the client (mawla) of so-and-so.")

* * *

Then He said, ﴿And there is no blame upon you for that in which you have made a mistake﴾, meaning the speaker's saying to another, "O my son," out of affection, and the speaker's saying to another, "O my father," out of respect, for this is like an error. Do you not see that the idle oath (laghw) in oaths is like error and a slip of the tongue? Likewise, a slip of the tongue in the speaker's saying, "my son," and the inadvertence in his saying "my son" without intending to establish lineage, are equal.

His saying, ﴿but [there is blame for] what your hearts intended﴾, is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, indicated by what preceded it, namely "blame," meaning: what your hearts intentionally did, in that there is blame.

﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾: He forgives sins and has mercy upon the sinner. We have mentioned a sufficient discussion on forgiveness and mercy in several places, and we will repeat some of it here, so we say: Forgiveness is that the Capable one withdraws the ugly deed issued by one under his power, to the extent that if a servant conceals his master's fault out of fear of his punishment, it is not said that he forgave him. Mercy is that he inclines toward him with kindness because of the helplessness of the one shown mercy, not in return for anything. For whoever inclines toward a capable person, such as a ruler, is not said to have shown him mercy. Likewise, whoever does good to another hoping for his benefit, or as a return for a kindness previously received from him, is not said to have shown him mercy. When this is known, forgiveness, when mentioned before mercy, its meaning is that he concealed his fault, then saw him bankrupt and helpless, so he showed him mercy and gave him what sufficed him. And when forgiveness is mentioned after mercy, which is rare, its meaning is that he inclined toward him because of his helplessness, so he left off his punishment and did not stop at that, but also concealed his sins.

[p. 169]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than they are to themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and those of relationship are closer to one another in the Book of Allah than the believers and the emigrants, except that you do kindness to your allies. That is written in the Book.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than they are to themselves﴾ is an affirmation of the validity of what came from him, upon him be blessings and peace, regarding his marriage to Zaynab. It is as though this is an answer to a question, namely that someone might say: "Grant that adopted sons are not sons, as you have said, but whoever named him a son, if his adopted son has something good that does not befit his manly honour to take from him, it is customarily reproached." So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers﴾ as an answer to that question. Its explanation is that the meeting of needs has degrees: first, meeting the need of strangers; then meeting the need of relatives on the outer edges of kinship; then meeting the need of the roots and branches (ascendants and descendants); then meeting the need of oneself. The first is, by custom, below the second, and likewise by the Law (shar'), for the 'aqilah (the paternal kin who bear the blood-money, diyah) bear the diyah for their own people and do not bear it for strangers. The second is below the third as well, which is obvious, by the evidence of maintenance (nafaqah). The third is below the fourth, for the self takes precedence over others. The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, pointed to this by his saying: "Begin with yourself, then with those you support."

[p. 169 continues]

When you know this, if a person has something with which he can cover one of his two legs, or with which he can meet a need of one side of his body, then if he takes the covering from one of them and covers the other with it, no one has the right to say to him, "Why did you do that?", let alone say, "How evil what you did is!" Unless one of the two limbs is more honourable than the other, as when a person shields his eye with his hand, and wards off cold from his head, which is the seat of his senses, and leaves his foot to be cold. That is what reason requires. So whoever reverses the matter is asked, "Why did you do that?" When this is clear, the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, is closer to the believer than his own self. So if the believer meets his own need and not the need of his Prophet, his example is like one who oils his hair and uncovers his head in extreme cold, intending to make his hair grow, while not knowing that he harms his head, from which alone his hair grows. Likewise, meeting the needs of the self is for the sake of its freedom to worship Allah, exalted is He, and there is no knowledge of how to worship except from the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. So if a person meets his need not for the sake of worship, it is not truly meeting a need, because meeting a need is that which goes beyond attaining a benefit, and this contains no benefit, let alone being a need. And if it is for worship, then leaving the Prophet, from whom one learns how to worship, in the matter of need and meeting the needs of the self, is like making hair grow while neglecting the head. Thus it becomes clear that when the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, wills something, it is forbidden for the community to oppose it, given its evident wisdom.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾. This is another affirmation. For Allah, exalted is He, placed the Prophet's wives in the ruling of mothers only so as to cut off the community's gaze from what the purpose of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, is attached to. So when his heart becomes attached to a woman, she shares with the wives in that attachment, and she becomes forbidden just as his wives are forbidden to others. If someone says: "How does He say, ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾, when He had said earlier, ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾, indicating that other than the one who bore a person does not become a mother in any way? And for this reason He said in another place, ﴿Their mothers are not but those who bore them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2]?" We say: His saying in the preceding verse, ﴿And Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way﴾, is an answer to this, and its meaning is that the Law is like reality. For this reason, when the reality cannot be taken into account, the intelligent person returns to the Law. Just as when two women each claim a particular child and have no evidence, and one of them swears and the other does not, the child is judged to belong to her; but if it becomes clear that the one who swore is below the age of puberty or is a virgin, by evidence, the child is not judged to belong to her. Thus it is known that when reality cannot be reached, one returns to the Law. Indeed, in some cases, rarely, the Law overrides reality, as when an adulterer is not made the father of a child born of adultery.

When this is established, the Lawgiver has the decision. So the saying of one who says, "This is my mother," is a statement that is understood not from reality and does not produce a reality. But the saying of the Lawgiver is true, and what confirms this is that the Lawgiver is the one by whom realities become realities, so He has the right to dispose of them. Do you not see that the mother did not become a mother except by Allah's creating the child in her womb? And if He had created it in the body of another, the mother would have been someone else. So when He is the one who makes the true mother a mother, He has the right to call a woman a mother and to give her the ruling of motherhood.

What is understood regarding the making of his wives our mothers is that Allah, exalted is He, made a father's wife forbidden to the son, because the wife is a place of jealousy and contention. For a son's marrying one who was under his father would lead to the severing of kinship and disobedience. But the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, is more noble and higher in rank than the father and more deserving of being pleased, for the father raises only in this world, while the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, raises in this world and the hereafter. So it was necessary that his wives be like the wives of fathers.

If someone says: "Why did He not say that the Prophet is your father, and this meaning would be achieved, or that his wives are the wives of your father?" We say: for a wisdom, which is that when we explained that if the Prophet wills the wife of one of the community, it is obligatory for that man to leave her so that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, may marry her; then if He had said, "He is your father," it would have made the wives of the believers forbidden to him forever. Also, because He made him closer to them than their own selves, and the self takes precedence over the father, by his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Begin with yourself, then with those you support." For this reason, one in need of food is not obliged to give it to his father, but he is obliged to give it to the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace. Furthermore, his wives have the ruling of the father's wives, so that their sons are not forbidden to the believers, nor their brothers, nor their mothers; although all of these are forbidden in the case of the true mother and the milk-mother.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and those of relationship are closer to one another in the Book of Allah than the believers and the emigrants, except that you do kindness to your allies. That is written in the Book.﴾ This refers to inheritance. And His saying, ﴿except that you do kindness to your allies﴾, refers to bequest. That is, if you make bequests, then non-heirs have a claim; but if you do not make bequests, then the heirs have the claim to your inheritance and to what you leave behind. If it is said: "Then, on this basis, what connection do inheritance and bequest have with what you mentioned?" We say: a strong, hidden connection that is not made clear except to one whom Allah has guided by His light. It is that someone other than the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, during his life, does not come to possess the property of others, and after his death his property does not pass to anyone other than his heirs. But the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, during his life, would come to possess the property of others when he willed it, and his property would not pass to his heirs after his death. It is as though Allah, exalted is He, compensated the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, for cutting off his inheritance by his power to take possession of others' property, and compensated the believers by the fact that what he left behind returns to them, so that there would be no hardship for the believers in the matter that when the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, wills something, it becomes his, then he dies and it remains for his heirs, so it is lost to them and does not return to them. Thus He said: ﴿and those of relationship are closer to one another﴾, meaning among you there is inheritance, so the property of one of you passes to another by inheritance, while the Prophet has no inheritance between himself and his relatives. So there should be in exchange for this that he is closer during his life to what is in your hands.

The second: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned an indication that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, is closer to the believers, namely that those of relationship are closer to one another. Then, if someone wishes to do good to a friend and bequeaths something to him, he becomes closer than his relative; it is as though by the bequest he has cut off inheritance and said, "This is my property, it passes from me only to whom I will." Likewise, Allah, exalted is He, made for His friend from the world what He willed, then whatever is left over goes to others. And His saying, ﴿That is written in the Book﴾, has two meanings.

One: in the Qur'an, namely the verses of inheritance and bequest.

The second: in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when We took from the Prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, and Abraham, and Moses, and Jesus son of Mary. And We took from them a solemn covenant.﴾

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when God, exalted is He, commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to be mindful of God, saying ﴿O Prophet, fear God﴾, and reinforced this with the account in which he feared people, so that he would fear no one but Him, and clarified that he had not committed anything that would warrant fear, by saying ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾, He reinforced it in another way and said ﴿And when We took from the Prophets﴾. It is as if He said: Fear God and do not fear anyone, and remember that God took the covenant of the Prophets that they would convey the messages of God, and that neither fear nor greed would prevent them from doing so. There are several issues here:

The first issue: what is meant by the covenant taken from the Prophets is their being sent and their being commanded to convey the message.

The second issue: He specifically mentioned four of the Prophets: Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. This is because Moses and Jesus had a people and a community in the time of our Prophet, so He mentioned them as an argument against their own peoples. As for Abraham, the Arabs used to affirm his virtue and followed him in some of the rites. As for Noah, it is because he was a second origin of mankind, since creation came into being from him after the Flood. On this basis, if someone says: then Adam should have been mentioned before Noah, we say: the creation of Adam was for the purpose of settling the earth, and his prophethood was like guidance for his children. For this reason, there was no destruction of a people or punishment in his time. As for Noah, he was created for prophethood and was sent as a warner, and for this reason his people were destroyed and drowned.

The third issue: In many places God says ﴿Jesus, son of Mary﴾ and ﴿the Messiah, son of Mary﴾, indicating that he had no father, for if he had one, he would have been identified by him. As for His saying ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾, the solemnity of the covenant is their being questioned about what they did in conveying the message, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will surely question those to whom messages were sent﴾ (Al-A'raf: 6). This is because when a king sends a messenger and commands him to do something, and he accepts it, that is a covenant. When he informs him that he will be questioned about his conduct in his actions and words, that is an intensification of the covenant upon him, so that he neither adds to nor subtracts from the message. On this basis, it is possible to say that what is meant by God's saying ﴿And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾ (An-Nisa': 21) is the information that they will be questioned about it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock." And just as God, exalted is He, made men guardians over women, He made the Prophets responsible for the affairs of their nations and for guiding them to the path of rectitude.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness. And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment.﴾

That is, He sent the messengers. The outcome for those who are accountable is either reckoning or punishment, because the truthful is called to account and the disbeliever is punished. This is like what ʿAlī, peace be upon him, said: "The world's lawful is a reckoning and its unlawful is a punishment." This necessitates general fear, and so His saying is reinforced: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾.

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when there came to you soldiers, and We sent upon them a wind and soldiers you did not see. And ever is Allah, of what you do, Seeing.﴾ ﴿When they came at you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah assumptions.﴾

This is a confirmation of the earlier command to fear Allah, to the extent that no fear of anyone remains with it. That is because the event of the gathering of the confederates and the intensification of the matter upon the Companions, when all the polytheists gathered together and all the Jews as one, and descended upon Madinah, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, dug the trench, the situation was at the utmost severity and fear reached its extreme. Allah repelled the people from them without fighting and granted them security from fear. Therefore the servant should not fear other than his Lord, for He suffices him in his affairs, and he should not feel safe from His plan, for He is capable of every possibility. He was able to overpower the Muslims by the disbelievers even though they were weak, just as He overpowered the disbelievers by the believers despite their strength and might. His saying: ﴿And We sent upon them a wind and soldiers you did not see﴾ is a reference to what Allah did to them: sending a cold wind upon them on a winter night, sending the angels, and casting terror into their hearts, so that some of them would cling to others out of fear of the horses in the depth of the night. The account is well known.

His saying: ﴿And ever is Allah, of what you do, Seeing﴾ is a reference to the fact that Allah knew your seeking refuge in Him and your hoping for His bounty, so He gave you victory over the enemies when you sought help. This is an affirmation of the obligation of fear and the impermissibility of fearing other than Allah, for His saying: ﴿We sent upon them a wind and soldiers you did not see﴾ means that Allah fulfills your need while you do not see. So if the face of security does not appear to you, do not be concerned by its non-appearance to you, because you do not see things; so do not fear other than Allah. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, so do not say that we do something while He does not see it. ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of everything.﴾

His saying: ﴿When they came at you from above you and from below you﴾ is an explanation of the severity of the matter and the extreme of fear. It has been said: "from above you" means from the direction of the east, and "from below you" means from the direction of the west, and they were the people of Makkah. ﴿And when the eyes shifted﴾ means they deviated from their normal course, so they did not turn toward the enemy because of its multitude. ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ is a metaphor for the utmost severity, because the heart, at anger, expands, and at fear, gathers and contracts, so it clings to the windpipe, and it may lead to blocking the passage of breath, so that a person cannot breathe and dies of fear. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then why not, when it reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 83].

His saying: ﴿And you assumed about Allah assumptions﴾: the alif and lam may be for totality, for emphasis, meaning you assumed every assumption; because at a great matter everyone assumes something. It may also be that the intended meaning is their customary assumptions, because what is customary from the believer is assuming good of Allah, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Assume good of Allah." And from the disbeliever is evil assumption, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾ [Ṣād: 27], and His saying: ﴿They follow not except assumption﴾ [Yūnus: 66]. If someone says: the verbal noun is not made plural, so what is the benefit of pluralizing ẓunūn (assumptions)? We say: there is no doubt that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, but a noun may be made to function as a verbal noun, as one says: "I struck him with whips" and "I disciplined him repeatedly." So it is as if He said: you assumed an assumption after an assumption, meaning you did not remain firm on one assumption. The benefit is that if Allah, exalted is He, had said "you assume an assumption," it would be possible that they were correct; but when He said ẓunūn, it became clear that among them were those whose assumption was false, because assumptions may all be false, and some of them may be false when they concern one matter. An example: if a group sees from afar a body, and some of them think it is Zayd, others think it is ʿAmr, and a third says it is Bakr, then when the truth becomes clear to them, all of them may be wrong and the seen object was a tree or a stone; or one of them may be correct, but it is not possible that all of them are correct. So His saying ﴿ẓunūn﴾ conveys that among them were those who erred in assumption; had He said "you assume an assumption about Allah," this meaning would not have been conveyed.

This is an affirmation of the obligation of fear and the impermissibility of fearing other than Allah, for His saying: ﴿We sent upon them a wind and soldiers you did not see﴾ means that Allah fulfills your need while you do not see. So if the face of security does not appear to you, do not be concerned by its non-appearance to you, because you do not see things; so do not fear other than Allah. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, so do not say that we do something while He does not see it. ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of everything.﴾

His saying: ﴿When they came at you from above you and from below you﴾ is an explanation of the severity of the matter and the extreme of fear. It has been said: "from above you" means from the direction of the east, and "from below you" means from the direction of the west, and they were the people of Makkah. ﴿And when the eyes shifted﴾ means they deviated from their normal course, so they did not turn toward the enemy because of its multitude. ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ is a metaphor for the utmost severity, because the heart, at anger, expands, and at fear, gathers and contracts, so it clings to the windpipe, and it may lead to blocking the passage of breath, so that a person cannot breathe and dies of fear. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then why not, when it reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 83].

His saying: ﴿And you assumed about Allah assumptions﴾: the alif and lam may be for totality, for emphasis, meaning you assumed every assumption; because at a great matter everyone assumes something. It may also be that the intended meaning is their customary assumptions, because what is customary from the believer is assuming good of Allah, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Assume good of Allah." And from the disbeliever is evil assumption, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾ [Ṣād: 27], and His saying: ﴿They follow not except assumption﴾ [Yūnus: 66]. If someone says: the verbal noun is not made plural, so what is the benefit of pluralizing ẓunūn (assumptions)? We say: there is no doubt that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, but a noun may be made to function as a verbal noun, as one says: "I struck him with whips" and "I disciplined him repeatedly." So it is as if He said: you assumed an assumption after an assumption, meaning you did not remain firm on one assumption. The benefit is that if Allah, exalted is He, had said "you assume an assumption," it would be possible that they were correct; but when He said ẓunūn, it became clear that among them were those whose assumption was false, because assumptions may all be false, and some of them may be false when they concern one matter. An example: if a group sees from afar a body, and some of them think it is Zayd, others think it is ʿAmr, and a third says it is Bakr, then when the truth becomes clear to them, all of them may be wrong and the seen object was a tree or a stone; or one of them may be correct, but it is not possible that all of them are correct. So His saying ﴿ẓunūn﴾ conveys that among them were those who erred in assumption; had He said "you assume an assumption about Allah," this meaning would not have been conveyed.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿There the believers were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking.﴾

That is, at that time God tested the believers, so that the truthful was distinguished from the hypocrite. And the testing by God is not for the purpose of making the matter clear to Him, but for another wisdom: God, exalted is He, knows what they are upon, but He wished to make the matter manifest to others, namely the angels and the prophets. This is like a master who knows that his slave will disobey him, and who has resolved to punish him for his disobedience, while in his presence are other slaves and others. So he orders him to do a task, knowing that he will disobey, and thus makes the matter clear to the others, and the punishment comes in the best manner, such that no one can say it was by injustice or from lack of forbearance.

And His saying ﴿and they were shaken﴾ means they were disturbed and stirred. Whoever among them held firm was among those of whom it is said: when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and by the remembrance of God they are at rest again. These are the believers in truth.

﴿And they had already covenanted with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs, and the covenant of Allah will be questioned.﴾ ﴿Say: Fleeing will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing, and then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little.﴾

This is an explanation of the corruption of their inner state and the ugliness of their conduct, for breaking their covenants. Then He threatened them with His saying: ﴿And the covenant of Allah will be questioned.﴾

Whatever Allah has decreed will occur. Whoever is commanded to do something and opposes it remains in the peril of punishment in the future and does not benefit from the opposition in the present. Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little.﴾ It is as if He says: even if you fled from it on this day, although that is not possible, you would not remain; rather, you would not be given enjoyment except for a little. The intelligent person does not desire a little thing when it causes him to miss a great deal. So there is no fleeing for you; and even if there were, you would not be given enjoyment after fleeing except for a little.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God knows those among you who hinder others, and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us," and who come to battle only a little.﴾

That is, those who discourage the Muslims and say, "Come to us, and do not fight with Muhammad (ﷺ)." Regarding this there are two views.

The first: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun) who used to say to the Ansar, "Do not fight, and hand Muhammad over to Quraysh."

The second: they are the Jews, who used to say to the people of Medina, "Come to us and be with us." The word ﴿halumma﴾ means "come" or "be present." In the dialect of the Hijaz it is not inflected, whereas in other dialects it is inflected: it is said to a group, "halummu," and to women, "halumma-n."

His saying ﴿and they do not come to battle except a little﴾ supports the first view, namely that the intended people are the hypocrites. This phrase admits of two meanings:

The first: ﴿they do not come to battle﴾ means they hold back from you and do not go out with you. In that case, God's saying ﴿stingy towards you﴾ means miserly, since they do not spend anything in the way of God.

The second: ﴿they do not come to battle﴾ means they do not fight alongside you, and they make excuses to avoid being occupied with fighting at the time of your presence with them. God's saying ﴿stingy towards you﴾ then means stingy with their own selves and bodies.

﴿Stingy towards you. So when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one who is overcome with fear of death. But when the fear departs, they lash you with sharp tongues, stingy towards the good. Those have not believed, so God has nullified their deeds. That is ever easy for God.﴾

This is an indication of the extreme of their cowardice and the depth of their terror. Know that stinginess resembles cowardice. Having mentioned stinginess, He explained its cause, which is cowardice. The evidence for this is that the coward is stingy with his wealth and does not spend it in the way of God, because he does not expect victory and so does not hope for spoils; he says, "This is an expenditure with no return," and so he hesitates over it. As for the brave man, he is certain of victory and of gaining booty, so it is easy for him to spend wealth in battle, out of hope for what is many times greater. Likewise with the self and the body: the coward fears his opponent, imagines failure, becomes timid and abandons advancing, whereas the brave man judges by victory and triumph, and so he advances.

God's saying ﴿when the fear departs, they lash you﴾ means they overpowered you with their tongues and harmed you with their speech, saying, "We are the ones who fought, and through us you were victorious, broke the enemy and prevailed." They demand the largest share of the spoils, though previously they had been content with the return (from the expedition) without any share of the spoils. God's saying ﴿stingy towards the good﴾: it has been said that "the good" means wealth. It is also possible to say its meaning is that they are scarce in good in both states and abundant in evil in both times: in the first they are stingy, and in the last they are likewise.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those have not believed, so God has nullified their deeds. That is ever easy for God.﴾ That is, they have not truly believed, even though they outwardly displayed belief, so God nullified the deeds they performed alongside the Muslims. God's saying ﴿That is ever easy for God﴾ is an indication of what appears in the eyes of the observer, as in His saying, ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. This is because nullification (ihbat) is annihilation and invalidation. When an observer considers the annihilation of bodies, he says that a body is dispersed into its parts; for whoever burns something leaves ashes behind, and this is because if the wind scatters the ashes, particles of them remain. This is the view of some people. The truth is that God annihilates bodies and restores whichever of them He wills. As for the deed, it is in reality nonexistent, although it remains in the sense that it persists by its ruling and its effects. So when it has no benefit and no consideration, it is nonexistent in reality and in ruling. Thus a deed that is not taken into account is nonexistent in reality, unlike the body.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Scripture who supported them from their fortresses, and cast terror into their hearts, a party you killed and a party you took captive.﴾

That is, those who supported them from among the People of the Scripture, and they were Banu Qurayza. ﴿From their fortresses﴾: from their strongholds. ﴿And cast terror into their hearts﴾: until they surrendered themselves to be killed, and their children and women to be taken captive. ﴿A party you killed﴾: and they were the men. ﴿And a party you took captive﴾: and they were the children and the women. If it is asked: is there a purpose in fronting the object (al-maf'ul) in His saying ﴿a party you killed﴾ and delaying it in His saying ﴿and a party you took captive﴾? I say: we have already answered that there is nothing in the Qur'an except that it has benefits, some of which are apparent and some of which are not. What appears from this, and God knows best, is that the speaker begins with what is more important, then what is better known, then what is closer. The men were well known, so killing fell upon them. The captives were the women and the young, who were not well known. Taking captive (al-sabyu wa al-asr) is more apparent than killing, because it remains, so it is evident to everyone that the person is a captive. So he fronted, of the two places, the one that is more apparent upon the act performed by it, and of the two verbs, he fronted the one that is more apparent over the less apparent place.

If we wish to state this in a manner that accords with the grammatical questions, we say: His saying ﴿a party you killed﴾ consists of a verb (fi'l) and an object (maf'ul). The basic principle in verbal sentences (al-jumal al-fi'liyyah) is that the verb is placed before the object and the subject. As for it being a verbal sentence: if it were a nominal sentence (ismiyyah), the required form for ﴿fariq﴾ would be the nominative (raf'), and he would have said "a party of them you kill them." Since it is in the accusative (nasb), it is by a suppressed verb (fi'l mudmar) that is explained by the apparent one, its estimate being "you kill a party, you kill." What drives this kind of speech is the intensity of concern with clarifying the object, and here too it is so, because when He mentioned the state of those who supported them, and that He had cast terror into their hearts, if He had said "you kill" and the hearer had to wait until he heard the object of "you kill," there would be a time interval, and something might intervene and prevent it, so it would not be known that they are the ones killed. But when He said "a party," the terror in their hearts having already preceded it in his hearing, he listens to the completion of the speech. And when the first (clause) consists of a verb and an object, the object is fronted for the purpose of coordinating the second clause upon it, on the original pattern. The non-fronting of the verb is because the reason for fronting has ceased when the state of those (captives) is known, and what comes after it is directed toward them. Had he said after that "and a party you take captive," whoever heard "a party" might suppose that it would be said of them that they are released, or that they are not under their control, so fronting the verb here is more appropriate. The same discussion applies to His saying ﴿and He brought down those who supported them﴾ and His saying ﴿and cast﴾, for the casting of terror was before the bringing down, because the terror became the cause of the bringing down. But since the joy in their bringing down was greater, the bringing down was fronted over the casting of terror, and God knows best.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And Allah is ever Able to do all things.﴾ ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release.﴾ ﴿But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode, then indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward.﴾

The connection is that noble character is confined to two things: magnifying the command of Allah, and compassion toward the creation of Allah. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this when he said: "The prayer, and what your right hands possess." Then, when Allah guided His Prophet to what relates to the side of magnifying Allah, by saying ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾, He mentioned what relates to the side of compassion, and began with the wives, for they are the people most deserving of compassion. For this reason He gave them precedence in maintenance.

In the verse there are juristic issues. Among them: was the giving of choice (al-takhyir, the offer to choose) obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) or not? We say: the giving of choice, as a statement, was undoubtedly obligatory, because it is conveying the message, since when Allah said to him, ﴿Say to them﴾, it became part of the message. As for the giving of choice in meaning, it depends on whether the command implies obligation or not. The apparent view is that it implies obligation.

Among them: if one of them chose separation, would her choice become separation (firaq, divorce)? The apparent view is that it does not become separation, but the one who chooses separates herself by a separation (ibana) from the side of the Prophet (ﷺ), based on His words, ﴿then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release﴾.

Among them: if one of them chose herself, and we say she is not separated except by a separation from the Prophet (ﷺ), was it obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) to divorce (talaq) or not? The apparent view, considering the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ), is that it was obligatory, because breaking a promise is not permissible for the Prophet, unlike for any one of us, for it is not binding upon him in the Law to fulfill what he promises.

Among them: after the irrevocable separation (bayna), would the one who was chosen be forbidden to others or not? The apparent view is that she would not be forbidden, otherwise the giving of choice would not have been possible for her, to enjoy the adornment of this world.

Among them: whoever chose Allah and His Messenger, was it forbidden for the Prophet (ﷺ), may the prayer and peace be upon him, to divorce her or not? The apparent view is that it is forbidden, considering the rank of the Messenger (ﷺ), in the sense that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not engage in it at all, meaning that if he did it he would be punished or reproached.

There are also verbal subtleties in it. Among them: the mention of choosing this world first, as an indication that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not turning toward their side even to the slightest degree, and how could he, when he is occupied with the worship of his Lord. Among them is His words, peace be upon him, ﴿and release you with a fair release﴾, an indication of what we have mentioned, for a fair release does not gather in custom with strong harm; so it is known that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not affected by their choosing separation from him, as evidenced by the fair release from him.

Among them is His words, ﴿But if you desire Allah﴾, informing them that in the choice of the Prophet (ﷺ) is the choice of Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode, and these three are the religion. His words, ﴿has prepared for the good-doers among you﴾, mean for whoever among you does righteous deeds. His words, ﴿desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode﴾, carry the meaning of faith. His words, ﴿for the good-doers﴾, explain excellence (ihsan), so that the verse is in meaning like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah while he is a doer of good﴾ [Luqman: 22], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever believes and does righteousness﴾ [al-Kahf: 88], and His words: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 82].

The great reward is the large one, excellent in its essence, good in its attributes, lasting through time. This is because "great" (azim) applied to bodies is only used for what is increased in length, width, and depth. If it is increased in length, it is called long (tawil); if increased in width, it is called wide (arid); likewise deep (amiq). When these three qualities are found together, it is called great (azim). So one says: a great mountain, when it is high and extended in all directions; if it is merely elevated, one says: a high mountain.

Having known this, the reward of this world is small in its essence, and in its attributes it is not free of aspects of ugliness, because of the harm and heaviness in what is eaten, likewise in what is drunk and in other pleasures; and it is not lasting. The reward of the Hereafter is abundant, free of aspects of ugliness, and lasting; therefore it is great.

Then He is Able to do all things; He can give you possession of other than them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And Allah is ever Able to do all things.﴾ ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release.﴾ ﴿But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode, then indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward.﴾

The connection is that noble character is confined to two things: magnifying the command of Allah, and compassion toward the creation of Allah. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this when he said: "The prayer, and what your right hands possess." Then, when Allah guided His Prophet to what relates to the side of magnifying Allah, by saying ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾, He mentioned what relates to the side of compassion, and began with the wives, for they are the people most deserving of compassion. For this reason He gave them precedence in maintenance.

In the verse there are juristic issues. Among them: was the giving of choice (al-takhyir, the offer to choose) obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) or not? We say: the giving of choice, as a statement, was undoubtedly obligatory, because it is conveying the message, since when Allah said to him, ﴿Say to them﴾, it became part of the message. As for the giving of choice in meaning, it depends on whether the command implies obligation or not. The apparent view is that it implies obligation.

Among them: if one of them chose separation, would her choice become separation (firaq, divorce)? The apparent view is that it does not become separation, but the one who chooses separates herself by a separation (ibana) from the side of the Prophet (ﷺ), based on His words, ﴿then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release﴾.

Among them: if one of them chose herself, and we say she is not separated except by a separation from the Prophet (ﷺ), was it obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) to divorce (talaq) or not? The apparent view, considering the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ), is that it was obligatory, because breaking a promise is not permissible for the Prophet, unlike for any one of us, for it is not binding upon him in the Law to fulfill what he promises.

Among them: after the irrevocable separation (bayna), would the one who was chosen be forbidden to others or not? The apparent view is that she would not be forbidden, otherwise the giving of choice would not have been possible for her, to enjoy the adornment of this world.

Among them: whoever chose Allah and His Messenger, was it forbidden for the Prophet (ﷺ), may the prayer and peace be upon him, to divorce her or not? The apparent view is that it is forbidden, considering the rank of the Messenger (ﷺ), in the sense that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not engage in it at all, meaning that if he did it he would be punished or reproached.

There are also verbal subtleties in it. Among them: the mention of choosing this world first, as an indication that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not turning toward their side even to the slightest degree, and how could he, when he is occupied with the worship of his Lord. Among them is His words, peace be upon him, ﴿and release you with a fair release﴾, an indication of what we have mentioned, for a fair release does not gather in custom with strong harm; so it is known that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not affected by their choosing separation from him, as evidenced by the fair release from him.

Among them is His words, ﴿But if you desire Allah﴾, informing them that in the choice of the Prophet (ﷺ) is the choice of Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode, and these three are the religion. His words, ﴿has prepared for the good-doers among you﴾, mean for whoever among you does righteous deeds. His words, ﴿desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode﴾, carry the meaning of faith. His words, ﴿for the good-doers﴾, explain excellence (ihsan), so that the verse is in meaning like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah while he is a doer of good﴾ [Luqman: 22], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever believes and does righteousness﴾ [al-Kahf: 88], and His words: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 82].

The great reward is the large one, excellent in its essence, good in its attributes, lasting through time. This is because "great" (azim) applied to bodies is only used for what is increased in length, width, and depth. If it is increased in length, it is called long (tawil); if increased in width, it is called wide (arid); likewise deep (amiq). When these three qualities are found together, it is called great (azim). So one says: a great mountain, when it is high and extended in all directions; if it is merely elevated, one says: a high mountain.

Having known this, the reward of this world is small in its essence, and in its attributes it is not free of aspects of ugliness, because of the harm and heaviness in what is eaten, likewise in what is drunk and in other pleasures; and it is not lasting. The reward of the Hereafter is abundant, free of aspects of ugliness, and lasting; therefore it is great.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear indecency, the punishment will be doubled for her, twofold; and that is easy for God.﴾

Indecency is ugly from them, and it is harder for the husband than anything else his wife might do. He threatened them with doubled punishment, and in this there are two wisdoms:

The first: the wife of another is punished for fornication because of the corruptions that fornication entails, and the wife of the Prophet is punished if she commits it for that reason as well, and for harming his heart and belittling his station. On this basis, the daughters of the Prophet (peace be upon him) are likewise. Also, if a woman were under the Prophet (ﷺ) and committed indecency, she would have chosen someone other than the Prophet (peace be upon him), and that other would be better and more deserving in her eyes than the Prophet. The Prophet is more deserving than the self, which is more deserving than others. So she has lowered the Prophet's station by two ranks, and she is punished with twice the punishment.

The second: this indicates their nobility, because the free woman's punishment is double the punishment of the slave woman, to show her honor. The relation of the Prophet to other men is like the relation of masters to slaves, since he is more deserving of them than their own selves. Likewise his wives and his close female relatives, who are the mothers of the believers. A person's mother is a woman who has authority over him and whose obedience is obligatory, and his wife is commanded, subject to his rule and under his obedience. Thus the wife of another, in relation to the wife of the Prophet (peace be upon him), becomes like a slave woman in relation to a free woman.

Know that the saying of the speaker "whoever does that" has the force of God's saying: ﴿If you associate others with God, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], in that it is possible to occur at first glance, and in some cases it definitely does not occur, and in some cases it definitely occurs—whoever dies has rested—and in some cases the listener hesitates between the two matters. So God's saying ﴿whoever of you commits indecency﴾ is, in our view, of the first type, for God has preserved the wives of the prophets from indecency. And God's saying ﴿and that is easy for God﴾ means: your being under the Prophet (peace be upon him) and your being noble and exalted is not something that repels punishment from you, and God's command is not like the command of creatures, where it is difficult for them to punish the honored because of their many allies, helpers, intercessors, and kinsmen.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever of you is obedient to God and His Messenger and does righteousness, We will give her her reward twice, and We have prepared for her a noble provision.﴾

Just as the generous, living person, when conferring benefit, reveals himself and his act, but when harm is involved does not mention himself. God's saying ﴿and We have prepared for her a noble provision﴾ describes the provision of the Hereafter as noble, although "noble" is only ever an attribute of the Provider, indicating a subtle meaning: provision in this world is determined through the hands of people. The merchant seeks provision from the market, and those who deal and craftsmen from those who use them, and rulers from the subjects, and subjects from them. So provision in this world does not come by itself; rather it is subjected to others who hold it back and send it to others. But in the Hereafter there is no sender or holder of it apparent, so it is what comes by itself. Therefore in this world only the Provider is described as noble, whereas in the Hereafter the provision itself is described as noble.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 33, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like anyone among women, if you are mindful of God. So do not be soft in speech, lest one in whose heart is a disease should be moved with desire, but speak in a known, proper manner.﴾

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like anyone among women.﴾ When He mentioned that their punishment is double the punishment of others and their reward is double the reward of others, they became like free women in comparison with slave women, so He said: ﴿You are not like anyone.﴾ The meaning of the saying of one who says, "So-and-so is not like ordinary people," is that he does not merely possess the quality of being a human being; rather, there is in him a more specific attribute, such as being a scholar, a worker, of noble lineage, or of honourable standing. When the more specific attribute is present, the description by the more general one no longer applies. For whoever knows a man and knows nothing of him beyond his being a man says, "I saw a man." But if he knows his knowledge, he says, "I saw Zayd or Amr." Likewise, the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿You are not like anyone among women⁠﻿﻿ means: there is in you something other than that, a matter that is not found in others, namely your being the mothers of all the believers and the wives of the best of the messengers. Just as Muhammad, peace be upon him, is not like anyone among men, as he, peace be upon him, said: "I am not like any of you," so too are his close kin who are honoured through him, and between spouses there is a kind of equality (kafa'ah).

Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are mindful of God, do not be soft in speech⁠﻿﻿ admits of two interpretations:

The first: that it is connected to what precedes it, with the meaning: "You are not like anyone, if you are mindful of God, for the most honoured in the sight of God is the most mindful."

The second: that it is connected to what follows it, with the meaning: "If you are mindful of God, then do not be soft in speech." When God forbade them from indecency, which is the ugly act, He forbade them from its preliminaries, which are conversing with men and yielding in speech to the sinner.

Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest one in whose heart is a disease⁠﻿﻿ means: one in whom there is corruption (fisq). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but speak in a known, proper manner⁠﻿﻿ means: the remembrance of God, and what you need of speech. When God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not be soft in speech,⁠﻿﻿ He mentioned after it ﴿but speak⁠﻿﻿, as an indication that this is not a command to harm or to do what is wrong; rather, proper speech, and speech when there is need, is what is commanded, and nothing else.

[p. 181]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And stay in your houses, and do not display yourselves in the manner of the display of the former Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance)﴾ ... ﴿and establish the prayer, and give the zakah, and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Stay in your houses﴾ is from al-qarar (staying in place). One of the two doubled letters is dropped, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَظَلْتُمْ تَفَكَّهُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65], meaning "so you would be left marveling." It has also been said that it comes from al-waqar (dignity), as one says "وَعَدَ يَعِدُ عِدْ" (the imperative of wa'ada, "to promise"), with the first letter dropped. His saying: ﴿and do not display yourselves in the manner of the display of the former Jahiliyyah﴾ has been said to mean: do not be coquettish and do not be flirtatious. It may also mean: do not show your adornment. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the former Jahiliyyah﴾ has two interpretations:

First: that what is meant is those who were in the time of Nuh (Noah), and the "other" Jahiliyyah is those who came after him.

Second: that "former" here does not imply a "later," but rather means the display of the ancient Jahiliyyah, as in the saying of the poet:

Where are the Akasirah (Persian kings), the tyrannical ones, and those (who were) ...
.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and establish the prayer, and give the zakah, and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾. That is: the obligation is not only in the prohibition, so that it is fulfilled by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَلا تَخْضَعْنَ﴾ [do not be soft in speech] and ﴿and do not display yourselves﴾. Rather, it is in the commands as well: ﴿and establish the prayer﴾, which is abandoning resemblance to the tyrant, the arrogant; ﴿and give the zakah﴾, which is resemblance to the generous, the merciful; ﴿and obey Allah﴾. That is: the obligation is not restricted to what has been mentioned. Rather, everything Allah has commanded, you should do, and everything Allah has forbidden, you should refrain from.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the House, and to purify you with a thorough purification﴾.

That is: the one who benefits from your obligations is not Allah, and you do not benefit Allah by what you do. Rather, the benefit is yours, and His command to you is for your own good. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to remove from you the impurity, O people of the House, and to purify you﴾ contains a subtle point, which is that impurity may be removed in essence while the place (of the heart) is not yet purified. So His saying: ﴿to remove from you the impurity﴾ means: He removes from you sins; ﴿and purify you﴾ means: He clothes you in the robes of honor. Furthermore, Allah, exalted is He, left addressing the feminine forms and addressed with the masculine address in His saying: ﴿to remove from you the impurity﴾, so that the women of His household and its men are included in it.

Opinions have differed concerning "the people of the House." The most preferable view is that it is said: they are his descendants and his wives, and al-Hasan and al-Husayn are among them, and Ali is among them, because he was of the people of his house by reason of his association with the Prophet's daughter and his constant companionship with the Prophet (ﷺ).

[Page 182]

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And remember what is recited in your homes of the signs of God and the wisdom﴾, that is, the Qur'an. ﴿And the wisdom﴾, that is, the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him), in reference to what we mentioned, that the obligations are not limited to prayer and zakat. What God mentioned in this verse, when He said ﴿And remember what is recited﴾, is so that they may know all the obligations and act upon them, and all the prohibitions in their entirety and refrain from them.

His saying ﴿Indeed, God is ever Subtle, Acquainted﴾ is an indication that He is acquainted with the hidden matters and subtle. His knowledge reaches everything, and among its meanings is the Subtle, who enters narrow passages and exits from closed paths.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women﴾. When He had commanded them and forbidden them, and explained what would be theirs, and mentioned to them ten levels. The first: Islam and submission to the command of God. The second: faith in what the command of God brings. For the obligated person at first says: "Whatever He says, I accept it." This is Islam. Then when God says something and he accepts it, he affirms His statement and corrects his belief, and this is faith. Then his belief calls him to good action and righteous deeds, so he becomes devout and worships. This is the third level, mentioned by His saying: ﴿And the devout men and devout women﴾. Then when he has believed and done righteous deeds, he becomes perfected, and he perfects others, enjoins what is good, and advises his brother, so he is truthful in his speech when giving counsel. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And the truthful men and truthful women﴾. Then whoever enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil is afflicted with harm, so he endures it, as God, exalted, said: ﴿And the patient men and patient women﴾. Then when he is perfected and perfects others, he may take pride in himself and be impressed by his worship, so He prevented him from that by His saying: ﴿And the humble men and humble women﴾. Or we may say: when He mentioned these good qualities, He pointed to what prevents them, which is either love of status or love of wealth, from external matters, or desire, from internal matters. Anger arises from these two, because it occurs due to loss of status, the forfeiture of wealth, or being prevented from a desired matter.

So His saying ﴿And the humble men and humble women﴾ means those who are humble, whom status does not turn away from worship. Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And the charitable men and charitable women﴾, meaning those who spend their wealth and do not hoard it out of their intense love for it. Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And the fasting men and fasting women﴾, an indication of those whom the appetite of the belly does not prevent from worshipping God. Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And the men who guard their chastity and the women who guard their chastity﴾, meaning those whom the sexual appetite does not prevent.

* * *

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And the men who remember God often and the women who remember Him﴾, meaning that they remember God in all these states, and their Islam, faith, devotion, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity and fasting are all with a sincere intention for God. Then He explained that his marriage to her, peace be upon him, although he was explaining a law that contains a benefit and was free of corruptions, is as follows: ﴿There is no discomfort upon the Prophet in what Allah has ordained for him.
